screens.subtitle: Establish Guardrails for Your Cloud Environment

narration.text: Welcome to this masterclass on enforcing compliance with Azure Policy. As organizations expand their presence in the cloud, maintaining control and ensuring adherence to standards across numerous subscriptions and resource groups becomes increasingly complex. Azure Policy is a critical service designed to address this challenge, acting as a powerful guardrail for your Azure environment. It allows you to define and enforce rules that your Azure resources must follow, ensuring consistency, security, and compliance with both internal requirements and external regulations. Throughout this chapter, you will learn how to leverage Azure Policy to proactively manage your cloud resources, prevent non-compliant deployments, and identify existing resources that violate your organizational rules. This capability is especially vital for large enterprises where multiple teams deploy resources, making consistent governance and security paramount. By the end, you'll understand how to implement robust governance strategies that scale with your cloud growth.

content.html:
Module 7›Chapter 7.6›What is Azure Policy?
Core Concept

What is Azure Policy?

Managing and enforcing organizational standards at scale.

The Cloud Guardrail

Azure Policy is a service that enables you to create, assign, and manage policies to enforce organizational standards and assess compliance across your Azure environment.

  • Enforce Standards: Define rules for resource configurations, ensuring consistency.
  • Assess Compliance: Continuously evaluate resources against policies to identify violations.
  • Prevent Non-Compliance: Stop resource creation or updates that violate rules.
  • Automate Governance: Manage policies at scale across multiple subscriptions and resource groups.
Key Takeaway

Azure Policy is your automated governance solution for maintaining a secure, consistent, and compliant cloud environment.

Why it Matters for Enterprises

For large organizations, manual compliance checks are unsustainable. Azure Policy provides:

  • Consistency: Ensures all resources adhere to a uniform configuration.
  • Security: Prevents deployments that introduce security vulnerabilities.
  • Compliance: Helps meet internal policies and external regulatory requirements.

Example Scenario

Imagine an organization requiring all virtual machines to have a 'Department' tag. Azure Policy can:

  • Audit: Report VMs missing the tag as non-compliant.
  • Deny: Prevent the creation of VMs without the required tag.
  • Modify: Automatically add the 'Department' tag if it's missing.

screens.title: The Three Pillars of Azure Policy
screens.subtitle: Policy Definitions, Initiatives, and Assignments.

narration.text: Azure Policy is built upon three fundamental concepts that work together to provide comprehensive governance: Policy Definitions, Initiatives, and Assignments. Think of these as the blueprint, the project plan, and the execution order for your cloud compliance strategy. First, Policy Definitions are the individual rules themselves. They specify what to evaluate on your resources and what action to take if a condition is met. For example, a definition might state, 'All storage accounts must use HTTPS.' Next, Initiatives, also known as Policy Set Definitions, are collections of these individual policy definitions grouped together to achieve a larger, overarching goal. Instead of assigning dozens of individual policies, you can assign a single initiative like 'Azure Security Baseline' which encompasses multiple related security policies. This significantly simplifies management and ensures a consistent application of a comprehensive set of rules. Finally, Assignments are the act of applying a policy definition or an initiative to a specific scope within your Azure environment, such as a management group, subscription, or resource group. This is where you decide where your rules will be enforced. Once assigned, Azure Policy continuously evaluates resources within that scope against the assigned rules, ensuring ongoing compliance. Understanding how these three pillars interact is key to effectively implementing and managing governance in Azure.

keyIdea.title: Policy Pillars
keyIdea.text: Azure Policy relies on Definitions (rules), Initiatives (collections of rules), and Assignments (applying rules to scope).

content.html:
Module 7›Chapter 7.6›Three Pillars
Core Concepts

The Three Pillars of Azure Policy

Policy Definitions, Initiatives, and Assignments.

1

Policy Definitions

JSON-based rules describing what to evaluate and what action to take (e.g., Deny, Audit).

Example

"Deny virtual machines without a specific tag."

2

Initiatives

Collections of policy definitions grouped to achieve a larger goal, simplifying management.

Example

"Azure Security Baseline" initiative includes multiple security policies.

3

Assignments

Applying a policy definition or initiative to a specific scope (e.g., subscription, resource group).

Example

Assigning a policy to your 'Production' resource group.

Key Takeaway

Definitions are the rules, Initiatives group them for scale, and Assignments apply them to your Azure environment.

screens.title: Anatomy of a Policy Definition
screens.subtitle: Understanding the JSON-based rules that drive compliance.

narration.text: At the heart of Azure Policy are Policy Definitions, which are JSON-based rules that precisely describe what to evaluate and what action to take. Each definition is a structured document that includes several key components. The mode specifies which resource types the policy applies to, such as all for all resources or indexed for resources that support tags and location, which is a common setting. Parameters offer flexibility, allowing you to reuse the same policy definition with different values, like specifying a particular tag name or allowed location. The core logic resides within the policy Rule, which contains an if condition and a then effect. The if condition defines what to evaluate, such as checking if a resource type is a storage account and if a specific property is set to false. If this condition is met, the then effect dictates the action. For example, a policy definition could be designed to audit any virtual machine that doesn't have a specific tag, or to deny the creation of a storage account that doesn't enforce HTTPS. This modular and declarative approach allows for highly granular control over your Azure resources, ensuring that your governance rules are clear, consistent, and enforceable across your entire cloud footprint.

keyIdea.title: JSON Rule Logic
keyIdea.text: Policy Definitions use JSON to define evaluation conditions (`if`) and resulting actions (`then`) for Azure resources.

content.html:
Module 7›Chapter 7.6›Policy Definition
Policy Structure

Anatomy of a Policy Definition

Understanding the JSON-based rules that drive compliance.

Key Components of a Definition

  • 1
    Mode: Specifies resource types to evaluate (e.g., all, indexed).
  • 2
    Parameters: Allows flexibility and reuse with dynamic values.
  • 3
    PolicyRule: Contains the core logic with if (condition) and then (effect).
Key Takeaway

Policy definitions are declarative JSON documents that define the 'what' and 'how' of your compliance rules.

JSON Policy Definition Structure
{
  "properties": {
    "displayName": "Required Tag Policy",
    "policyType": "Custom",
    "mode": "Indexed",
    "description": "Ensures resources have a 'CostCenter' tag.",
    "parameters": {
      "tagName": {
        "type": "String",
        "metadata": {
          "displayName": "Tag Name",
          "description": "Name of the tag to enforce"
        },
        "defaultValue": "CostCenter"
      }
    },
    "policyRule": {
      "if": {
        "field": "tags.[parameters('tagName')]",
        "exists": "false"
      },
      "then": {
        "effect": "Audit"
      }
    }
  }
}

screens.title: Understanding Policy Effects
screens.subtitle: The actions Azure Policy takes when rules are met.

narration.text: When a policy rule's if condition is met, the then effect dictates the action Azure Policy will take. These effects are crucial for defining how strictly your governance rules are enforced. The Deny effect is the most restrictive; it prevents the creation or update of any resource that violates the policy. For example, if you have a Deny policy against creating virtual machines in a specific region, any attempt to deploy a VM there will simply fail. In contrast, the Audit effect is less intrusive. It allows non-compliant resources to be created or updated but generates a warning in the compliance report, providing visibility without blocking operations. This is excellent for initial policy rollouts or for monitoring. The Deploy If Not Exists effect is powerful for automation; if a condition isn't met, it automatically deploys a specified resource or configuration. For instance, if a VM is created without a required diagnostic setting, Deploy If Not Exists can add it. Similarly, the Modify effect changes properties of a resource to bring it into compliance, such as adding a missing tag or updating a network security group rule. Understanding these distinct effects is vital for designing policies that align with your organizational needs, balancing strict enforcement with operational flexibility. A common misconception is that Audit will eventually block, but it only reports; you need Deny for hard stops.

keyIdea.title: Actionable Outcomes
keyIdea.text: Policy effects like Deny, Audit, DeployIfNotExists, and Modify define how Azure Policy responds to non-compliance.

content.html:
Module 7›Chapter 7.6›Policy Effects
Policy Effects

Understanding Policy Effects

The actions Azure Policy takes when rules are met.

Deny

Prevents resource creation or update if it violates the policy rule. This is a hard stop for non-compliance.

Example

Block VMs deployed in unauthorized regions.

Audit

Warns about non-compliance but allows resource creation/update. Provides visibility without blocking.

Example

Report storage accounts not enforcing HTTPS.

DeployIfNotExists

Deploys a resource or configuration if a condition isn't met. Automates remediation.

Example

Add diagnostic settings to VMs if missing.

Modify

Changes properties of a resource to bring it into compliance. Requires a managed identity.

Example

Add a specific tag to resources if missing.

Key Takeaway

Choose the right effect to balance strict enforcement with operational flexibility and automated remediation.

screens.title: Initiatives: Grouping Policies for Scale
screens.subtitle: Collections of policy definitions for broader governance goals.

narration.text: While individual policy definitions are powerful, managing numerous policies can become cumbersome. This is where Initiatives, also known as Policy Set Definitions, come into play. An initiative is essentially a collection of policy definitions grouped together to achieve a larger, more comprehensive governance goal. For instance, instead of assigning multiple individual policies like 'Enforce MFA,' 'Encrypt Storage,' and 'Log Network Activity,' you can create a single initiative named 'Azure Security Baseline.' This initiative would then encompass all these related security policies. The primary benefit of initiatives is simplification. By assigning a single initiative, you ensure that a comprehensive set of rules is applied consistently across your chosen scope, rather than having to manage and assign each policy individually. This not only streamlines the administrative process but also reduces the chance of overlooking a critical policy. Initiatives are particularly useful for implementing industry standards or internal compliance frameworks that require multiple interdependent rules. They act as a logical container, making your governance strategy more organized and easier to scale as your cloud environment grows. A common mistake is to create too many individual policies when an initiative could group them more effectively.

keyIdea.title: Simplified Management
keyIdea.text: Initiatives group multiple policy definitions to achieve broader governance goals, simplifying assignment and management.

content.html:
Module 7›Chapter 7.6›Initiatives
Policy Grouping

Initiatives: Grouping Policies for Scale

Collections of policy definitions for broader governance goals.

What are Initiatives?

Initiatives, or Policy Set Definitions, are logical groupings of multiple policy definitions. They allow you to manage and assign a comprehensive set of rules as a single unit.

  • Simplify Management: Assign one initiative instead of many individual policies.
  • Achieve Broader Goals: Combine policies for security, cost management, or operational excellence.
  • Consistent Application: Ensures all related rules are applied uniformly.
Key Takeaway

Use initiatives to streamline policy management and apply comprehensive governance frameworks efficiently.

Example: Azure Security Baseline

An initiative like "Azure Security Baseline" can include policies such as:

  • Enforce MFA: Requires multi-factor authentication for all users.
  • Encrypt Storage: Ensures all storage accounts use encryption.
  • Log Network Activity: Mandates logging for network security groups.
  • Restrict Public IPs: Prevents creation of public IP addresses on VMs.

Benefits of Using Initiatives

  • Reduced Administrative Overhead: Fewer assignments to manage.
  • Holistic Compliance: Ensures a complete set of rules is applied.
  • Improved Readability: Clearer understanding of governance goals.

screens.title: Policy Assignments: Applying Rules to Scope
screens.subtitle: Defining where and how policies are enforced in Azure.

narration.text: Once you've defined your policies or grouped them into initiatives, the next critical step is to apply them to your Azure environment through Policy Assignments. An assignment is the act of taking a policy definition or an initiative and applying it to a specific scope. This scope can be broad, such as an entire management group or subscription, or more granular, like a particular resource group. When you create an assignment, you specify which definition or initiative to use, the target scope, and optionally, any parameter values that customize the policy's behavior. For example, if you have a policy that audits resources without a 'Department' tag, you might assign it to your 'Development' subscription and set the 'Department' parameter to 'Engineering' for that specific assignment. Once assigned, Azure Policy continuously evaluates all resources within that defined scope against the assigned rules. This evaluation happens both for new or updated resources, which are checked at the time of creation or modification, and for existing resources, which are periodically re-evaluated. This continuous assessment ensures that your environment remains compliant over time, providing ongoing governance and security. Understanding scope is vital; policies inherit down the hierarchy, meaning a policy assigned at a management group will apply to all subscriptions and resource groups beneath it, unless explicitly excluded.

keyIdea.title: Scope-Based Enforcement
keyIdea.text: Policy Assignments apply definitions or initiatives to specific scopes (management group, subscription, resource group) for continuous evaluation.

content.html:
Module 7›Chapter 7.6›Assignments
Policy Deployment

Policy Assignments: Applying Rules to Scope

Defining where and how policies are enforced in Azure.

What is an Assignment?

An assignment is the act of applying a policy definition or an initiative to a specific scope within your Azure hierarchy. This activates the policy's rules for resources within that scope.

  • Target Scope: Can be a management group, subscription, or resource group.
  • Parameter Values: Customize policy behavior for specific assignments.
  • Continuous Evaluation: Resources are checked against rules at creation/update and periodically.
Key Takeaway

Assignments are the activation point for your policies, defining their reach and impact within your Azure hierarchy.

Understanding Scope Hierarchy

Policies inherit down the Azure resource hierarchy. Be mindful of:

  • Management Group: Policies apply to all subscriptions and resource groups within it.
  • Subscription: Policies apply to all resource groups and resources within that subscription.
  • Resource Group: Policies apply to all resources within that specific resource group.

Practical Example

To ensure all storage accounts in your 'Production' subscription enforce HTTPS, you would:

  • Create or select a policy definition for HTTPS enforcement.
  • Assign this policy to the 'Production' subscription.
  • All new and existing storage accounts in that subscription will be evaluated.

screens.title: Enforcing HTTPS for Storage Accounts
screens.subtitle: Creating a custom policy definition and assigning it via Azure CLI.

narration.text: Let's walk through a practical example of creating a custom Azure Policy to enforce secure transfer, specifically HTTPS only, for all storage accounts. This is a common security requirement for many organizations. We'll define a policy that audits any storage account where the supports Https Traffic Only property is set to false. The JSON structure for this policy definition is quite straightforward. It specifies a display name, sets the policy type to 'Custom,' and defines the mode as 'Indexed' because storage accounts support tags and location. The policy Rule then uses an if condition to check two things: first, if the resource type is a storage account, and second, if its supports Https Traffic Only property is false. If both conditions are true, the then effect is set to Audit, meaning it will report non-compliance without blocking the resource. If you wanted to prevent such storage accounts from being created or updated, you would simply change the effect to Deny. After defining this JSON, you would use the Azure CLI to create the policy definition in Azure and then assign it to your desired scope, such as a specific subscription or resource group. This process demonstrates how you can translate a clear organizational standard into an automated governance rule, ensuring secure configurations across your cloud resources.

keyIdea.title: Policy-as-Code
keyIdea.text: Custom policies are defined in JSON and deployed via CLI to enforce specific organizational standards like HTTPS-only for storage.

content.html:
Module 7›Chapter 7.6›Custom Policy
Custom Policy Example

Enforcing HTTPS for Storage Accounts

Creating a custom policy definition and assigning it via Azure CLI.

Policy Definition Explained

This JSON policy definition audits storage accounts that do not enforce HTTPS-only traffic. It targets Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts and checks the supportsHttpsTrafficOnly property.

  • Target: Storage accounts (Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts).
  • Condition: supportsHttpsTrafficOnly is false.
  • Effect: Audit (reports non-compliance). Change to Deny to block.
Key Takeaway

Custom policies allow precise control over resource configurations, enabling automated enforcement of security standards.

Custom Policy Definition (audit-https.json)
{
  "properties": {
    "displayName": "Storage accounts should use HTTPS only",
    "policyType": "Custom",
    "mode": "Indexed",
    "description": "This policy ensures that all storage accounts enforce HTTPS traffic only.",
    "policyRule": {
      "if": {
        "allOf": [
          {
            "field": "type",
            "equals": "Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts"
          },
          {
            "field": "Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/supportsHttpsTrafficOnly",
            "equals": false
          }
        ]
      },
      "then": {
        "effect": "Audit"
      }
    }
  }
}

screens.title: Compliance Reports and Remediation Tasks
screens.subtitle: Monitoring policy adherence and automatically fixing non-compliant resources.

narration.text: After policies are assigned, monitoring their effectiveness is crucial. Azure Policy provides comprehensive compliance reports in the Azure portal, giving you a clear overview of which resources are compliant, non-compliant, or exempt from your rules. This report acts as your dashboard for governance, highlighting areas that require attention. For any resources identified as non-compliant, you can initiate remediation tasks. Remediation is the process of bringing non-compliant resources back into compliance. For policies with Deploy If Not Exists or Modify effects, remediation can be automated. For example, if a Deploy If Not Exists policy detects a virtual machine without a required diagnostic setting, a remediation task can automatically deploy that setting. Similarly, a Modify policy can automatically add a missing tag to a resource. For Audit policies, remediation typically involves manual steps or a separate Deploy If Not Exists policy to deploy a missing resource, as Audit itself doesn't alter resources. It's important to understand that remediation tasks are not instantaneous; they run in the background and may take some time to complete, especially for a large number of resources. Regularly reviewing compliance reports and acting on remediation tasks ensures that your Azure environment consistently adheres to your defined governance requirements, maintaining a strong security posture and operational consistency.

keyIdea.title: Monitor & Fix
keyIdea.text: Compliance reports show policy adherence, and remediation tasks automatically or manually fix non-compliant resources.

content.html:
Module 7›Chapter 7.6›Compliance & Remediation
Compliance Management

Compliance Reports and Remediation Tasks

Monitoring policy adherence and automatically fixing non-compliant resources.

Understanding Compliance Reports

The Azure Policy compliance report provides a dashboard view of your resources' adherence to assigned policies. It categorizes resources as:

  • Compliant: Resources that meet all policy rules.
  • Non-Compliant: Resources that violate one or more policy rules.
  • Exempt: Resources explicitly excluded from policy evaluation.
Key Takeaway

Regularly review compliance reports and utilize remediation tasks to maintain a compliant and secure Azure environment.

Initiating Remediation Tasks

Remediation tasks bring non-compliant resources into compliance. Their behavior depends on the policy effect:

  • DeployIfNotExists / Modify: Remediation can automatically deploy missing resources or modify properties.
  • Audit: Remediation typically involves manual intervention or a separate policy with an automated effect.

Example: Automated Remediation

If a policy requires all VMs to have a specific diagnostic setting, and a VM is found without it:

  • A DeployIfNotExists policy identifies the non-compliant VM.
  • A remediation task is initiated to automatically deploy the missing diagnostic setting.
  • The VM is then brought into compliance without manual intervention.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Safety Notes
screens.subtitle: Avoiding pitfalls when implementing Azure Policy.

narration.text: While Azure Policy is a powerful governance tool, it's essential to be aware of common mistakes and safety considerations to avoid operational disruptions. One significant pitfall is deploying overly broad Deny policies. Applying a Deny effect at a high scope, such as an entire subscription, without thorough testing can inadvertently block legitimate deployments and cause widespread issues. Always test Deny policies in a controlled environment first. Another common error is ignoring Audit results. Audit policies provide valuable visibility into non-compliance, but if you don't act on these reports, their value diminishes significantly. It's crucial to establish a process for reviewing and addressing audit findings. Misunderstanding policy effects can also lead to unexpected behavior. For instance, Deploy If Not Exists policies require a managed identity for the policy assignment to have the necessary permissions to deploy resources. Without it, the policy won't function as intended. Finally, be mindful of scope issues and inheritance. Policies inherit down the hierarchy, so a policy assigned at a management group applies to all child subscriptions and resource groups. Use exclusions (not Scopes) sparingly and with clear justification, as they can create governance gaps. The safest approach is to always start with Audit effects, thoroughly test your policies, and gradually transition to Deny or Modify as your confidence grows. This iterative approach minimizes risk and ensures your policies achieve their intended governance goals without causing unintended side effects.

keyIdea.title: Policy Pitfalls
keyIdea.text: Avoid broad Deny policies, act on Audit results, understand effects, and manage scope carefully to prevent operational issues.

content.html:
Module 7›Chapter 7.6›Safety Notes
Best Practices

Common Mistakes and Safety Notes

Avoiding pitfalls when implementing Azure Policy.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Overly broad Deny policies: Can block legitimate deployments.
  • Ignoring Audit results: Reduces the value of visibility policies.
  • Misunderstanding effects: Each effect has specific requirements (e.g., managed identity for DeployIfNotExists).
  • Scope issues: Policies inherit; exclusions can create gaps.
Key Takeaway

Start with Audit, test thoroughly, and gradually transition to stricter effects to ensure safe and effective governance.

Safety Notes for Policy Deployment

  • Test in Controlled Environments: Always validate policies before broad deployment.
  • Start with Audit: Gain visibility before enforcing stricter effects.
  • Use Exclusions Sparingly: Only with clear justification to avoid governance gaps.

Pro-Tip: Gradual Rollout

Implement policies in phases:

  • Phase 1: Deploy with Audit effect to understand impact.
  • Phase 2: Introduce DeployIfNotExists or Modify for automated remediation.
  • Phase 3: Apply Deny for critical, well-understood violations.

screens.title: Creating a Custom Policy for Storage Encryption
screens.subtitle: Defining and deploying a custom policy via Azure CLI.

narration.text: Now, let's get hands-on and create a custom Azure Policy definition to audit storage accounts that do not have blob service encryption enabled. While new storage accounts typically have this enabled by default, this exercise demonstrates the process of defining and deploying a custom policy. First, we'll create a dedicated resource group to contain our policy demo resources, ensuring a clean environment for testing. Then, we'll define our custom policy in a JSON file. This policy will specifically look for storage accounts where the encryption. services. blob. enabled property is set to false, and if found, it will trigger an Audit effect. This means it will report these accounts as non-compliant without preventing their creation. Once the JSON definition is ready, we'll use the Azure CLI to create this custom policy definition within Azure. This command takes our JSON file and registers the policy with your Azure subscription. This step is crucial as it makes your custom rule available for assignment. This process illustrates how you can translate a specific security or compliance requirement into a tangible, enforceable policy within your Azure environment, providing a foundation for automated governance. Remember, the Audit effect is ideal for initial deployment to understand the impact before moving to stricter enforcement.

keyIdea.title: Policy Definition via CLI
keyIdea.text: Create a resource group, define a custom JSON policy for storage encryption audit, and deploy it using Azure CLI.

content.html:
Module 7›Chapter 7.6›Hands-on Policy
Hands-on Activity

Creating a Custom Policy for Storage Encryption

Defining and deploying a custom policy via Azure CLI.

Steps Overview

  1. Create a dedicated Resource Group for the demo.
  2. Define the custom policy in a JSON file to audit storage encryption.
  3. Create the custom policy definition in Azure using Azure CLI.
Key Takeaway

The Azure CLI provides a powerful way to programmatically define and deploy custom policies for automated governance.

Azure CLI Commands
# 1. Create a Resource Group
RG_NAME="PolicyDemoRG"
LOCATION="eastus"
az group create --name $RG_NAME --location $LOCATION

# 2. Create Custom Policy Definition (audit-storage-encryption.json)
# (Content for this file is provided in the previous screen's JSON)

# 3. Create the Custom Policy Definition in Azure
POLICY_DEF_NAME="AuditStorageEncryption"
az policy definition create \
    --name $POLICY_DEF_NAME \
    --display-name "Audit Storage Accounts without Blob Service Encryption" \
    --description "Audits storage accounts that do not have encryption enabled for blob services." \
    --rules audit-storage-encryption.json \
    --mode Indexed

screens.title: Assigning the Custom Policy and Testing Compliance
screens.subtitle: Applying the policy and observing its effect on a new resource.

narration.text: With our custom policy definition created, the next step is to assign it to a specific scope and then observe its effect. We'll use the Azure CLI to create a policy assignment, linking our Audit Storage Encryption policy to the resource group we created earlier. This command specifies the policy definition by name, the target scope, and any parameters required by the policy, in this case, setting the effect to Audit. Once assigned, Azure Policy will begin evaluating resources within that resource group. To test this, we'll then create a new storage account within the same resource group. By default, new storage accounts have blob service encryption enabled, so our policy should report this new account as compliant. This step is crucial for verifying that your policy is correctly configured and actively monitoring your resources. After creating the storage account, you would typically navigate to the Azure portal, search for 'Policy,' and then go to the 'Compliance' section. It's important to remember that it can take 10 to 20 minutes for the compliance scan to run and for the results to appear in the portal. Refreshing the page periodically will show the updated compliance status. This entire process, from definition to assignment and verification, demonstrates the full lifecycle of implementing a custom Azure Policy for governance.

Module 7›Chapter 7.6›Hands-on Policy
Hands-on Activity

Assigning the Custom Policy and Testing Compliance

Applying the policy and observing its effect on a new resource.

Steps Overview

  1. Assign the custom policy to your Resource Group using Azure CLI.
  2. Create a Storage Account within the Resource Group to test compliance.
  3. Review compliance status in the Azure Portal (allow 10-20 minutes for scan).
Key Takeaway

Policy assignments activate your rules, and compliance reports provide essential feedback on their effectiveness.

Azure CLI Commands
# 4. Assign the Custom Policy to your Resource Group
POLICY_ASSIGN_NAME="AuditStorageEncryptionAssignment"
az policy assignment create \
    --name $POLICY_ASSIGN_NAME \
    --display-name "Audit Storage Accounts without Blob Service Encryption Assignment" \
    --scope /subscriptions/$(az account show --query id -o tsv)/resourceGroups/$RG_NAME \
    --policy $POLICY_DEF_NAME \
    --params "{ \"effect\": { \"value\": \"Audit\" } }"

# 5. Create a Storage Account (to test compliance)
STORAGE_ACCOUNT_NAME="policydemostorage$(head /dev/urandom | tr -dc a-z0-9 | head -c 10)" # Unique name
az storage account create \
    --name $STORAGE_ACCOUNT_NAME \
    --resource-group $RG_NAME \
    --location $LOCATION \
    --sku Standard_LRS \
    --kind StorageV2

# 6. Review Compliance (Azure Portal - conceptual step)
# Navigate to Azure portal -> Policy -> Compliance. Refresh after 10-20 mins.

screens.title: Key Concepts: Foundations of Azure Policy
screens.subtitle: Essential terms for enforcing cloud governance.

narration.text: As we conclude this chapter, let's recap the foundational concepts of Azure Policy. First, remember that Azure Policy itself is the service that empowers you to create, assign, and manage policies to enforce organizational standards and assess compliance at scale. It's your central hub for cloud governance. Next, we have Policy Definitions, which are the JSON-based rules that form the core logic of your policies. These definitions describe the conditions for evaluation and the specific effect to take if those conditions are met, such as auditing or denying a resource. Finally, Initiatives, also known as Policy Set Definitions, are crucial for managing complexity. They are collections of multiple policy definitions grouped together to achieve a single, larger goal, like an entire security baseline. Understanding these three concepts is fundamental to building an effective and scalable governance strategy in Azure. They work in concert to ensure your cloud environment remains consistent, secure, and compliant with your organizational requirements.

keyIdea.title: Core Policy Elements
keyIdea.text: Azure Policy, Definitions, and Initiatives are the building blocks for scalable cloud governance.

content.html:
Module 7›Chapter 7.6›Key Concepts

Key Concepts: Foundations of Azure Policy

Essential terms for enforcing cloud governance.

Azure Policy

A service to create, assign, and manage policies for enforcing organizational standards and assessing compliance at scale.

Policy Definition

A JSON-based rule describing conditions for evaluation and the effect to take if conditions are met.

Initiative

A collection of policy definitions grouped together to achieve a single, larger governance goal.

Summary Takeaway

Azure Policy provides the framework, definitions are the rules, and initiatives organize those rules for effective cloud governance.

screens.title: Key Concepts: Policy Implementation & Monitoring
screens.subtitle: Understanding how policies are applied and managed.

narration.text: Continuing our review of key concepts, let's focus on how policies are put into action and monitored. Policy Assignment is the crucial step where you apply a policy definition or an initiative to a specific scope, such as a management group, subscription, or resource group. This is where your rules become active within your Azure environment. Next, Policy Effects define the action taken when a policy rule is met. These effects range from Deny, which blocks non-compliant operations, to Audit, which simply reports non-compliance, and Deploy If Not Exists or Modify, which can automatically remediate issues. Understanding these effects is vital for choosing the right enforcement strategy. Finally, the Compliance Report is your dashboard in Azure Policy, showing the compliance status of your resources against assigned policies. It helps you identify non-compliant resources and track overall adherence. When non-compliance is found, a Remediation Task is an action taken to bring those resources back into compliance, often automated for Deploy If Not Exists or Modify policies. These concepts collectively enable you to implement, monitor, and maintain a compliant and well-governed Azure cloud environment.

keyIdea.title: Policy Lifecycle
keyIdea.text: Assignments activate policies, effects define actions, and compliance reports with remediation ensure ongoing adherence.
